title: Databases and Data Modelling
summary: Learn relational databases: tables and keys, entity-relationship modelling, normalisation, SQL with constraints and joins, indexes and transactions, and when to choose NoSQL. Every query result was checked by running it.
audience: IT and computer science students, developers, analysts and anyone building data systems

body.p: A database is an organised collection of data, managed by a database management system (DBMS) that lets many users and programs store, find and change data safely at the same time. Banks, hospitals, schools, online shops and mobile-money services all run on databases.

list: Duplicated data: the same customer typed into many sheets, slightly differently each time.
Inconsistency: an address updated in one place but not another.
Weak rules: nothing stops a negative price or a missing ID.
Concurrency: two people editing the same file overwrite each other.
Security: hard to give each user access to only part of the data.

body.p: A DBMS solves these with structured tables, rules (constraints), a query language, permissions, backups and transactions. Popular relational systems include PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server and Oracle; NoSQL systems such as MongoDB and Redis suit some other workloads.

body.tip: If several people or programs need the same data and it must stay correct, it probably belongs in a database rather than a spreadsheet.

body.p: In a relational database, data lives in tables (relations) of rows and columns. Each column has a data type, such as INTEGER, TEXT or DATE. Each row describes one thing: one student, one course, one enrolment.

list: Primary key: a column (or set of columns) that uniquely identifies each row, such as student id. It can never be empty or duplicated.
Foreign key: a column that refers to a primary key in another table, linking the tables, such as enrolments.student_id referring to students.id.
Candidate keys are other columns that could also be unique, such as a national ID number.
Surrogate keys are invented IDs (1, 2, 3…) used instead of real-world values that might change.
One-to-one: each person has one passport record.
One-to-many: one school has many students; put the foreign key on the "many" side.
Many-to-many: students take many courses and courses have many students; this needs a junction table, such as enrolments, holding both foreign keys.

body.tip: Never use names as keys. Two students called Chidi Okafor will eventually enrol.

body.p: Before creating tables, model the data. An entity-relationship (ER) diagram shows entities (things you store data about), their attributes and the relationships between them, with cardinality (one or many) on each end.

list: List the nouns in the requirements: student, course, school, teacher. These are candidate entities.
List facts about each: a student has a name and school; a course has a code and title.
Find the verbs linking them: a student enrols in a course.
Decide the cardinality: a student can enrol in many courses, and a course can have many students, so it is many-to-many.
Add attributes that belong to the relationship itself, such as the grade, which belongs to an enrolment, not to the student or the course alone.

body.tip: Check the model by asking real questions of it: "Which students took Mathematics, and what did they score?" If the model cannot answer, it is missing something.

body.p: Normalisation organises tables so that each fact is stored once. This prevents update anomalies (changing data in one row but not others), insertion anomalies (being unable to add a course until someone enrols) and deletion anomalies (losing a course's title when its last student leaves).

list: First normal form (1NF): every cell holds a single value; no lists such as "MAT, PHY" in one cell and no repeating columns such as course1, course2.

Second normal form (2NF): in a table with a composite key, every non-key column depends on the whole key. A course title depends only on the course code, so it moves out of the enrolments table into the courses table.

Third normal form (3NF): non-key columns depend only on the key, not on other non-key columns. If a students table held school and school_phone, the phone depends on the school, so it belongs in a schools table.

body.p: A useful summary: every non-key attribute must depend on the key, the whole key and nothing but the key. Data warehouses sometimes deliberately denormalise (duplicate data) to make reporting faster, but they do so knowingly.

body.tip: If you find yourself correcting the same value in many rows, the design probably needs another table.

body.p: SQL defines structures (CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE) and works with data (INSERT, SELECT, UPDATE, DELETE). Constraints make the database enforce rules: NOT NULL, UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY and CHECK.
Three students (Ama, Chidi, Wanjiru), four courses (Mathematics, Physics, Biology, Chemistry) and five enrolments: Ama MAT 78 and PHY 65, Chidi MAT 82, Wanjiru BIO 90 and MAT 71.

list: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM enrolments returns 5.
Joining students to enrolments, ordering Mathematics grades from highest and taking one row returns Chidi (82).
Grouping by course: BIO 1 student averaging 90, MAT 3 averaging 77, PHY 1 averaging 65.
A LEFT JOIN from courses to enrolments, keeping rows with no match, finds courses nobody takes: Chemistry.
Inserting Ama into MAT a second time fails (primary key), and a grade of 120 fails the CHECK constraint.

body.p: These results were produced by running the SQL. Letting the database enforce rules is far more reliable than hoping every program checks them.

body.tip: Write constraints first, then try to insert bad data on purpose. If the database accepts it, add a rule.

body.p: An index is like a book's index: it lets the database find rows without reading the whole table. Finding one row among 1 000 000 by scanning takes about 500 000 comparisons on average; a B-tree index needs only a few steps (a balanced binary search would need about log₂ 1 000 000, about 20). Indexes speed up reads but slow writes slightly and use space, so index the columns you search and join on.

list: Atomicity: all steps of a transaction happen, or none do. A money transfer debits one account and credits another together.
Consistency: every transaction leaves the data valid under the rules.
Isolation: simultaneous transactions do not see each other's half-finished work.
Durability: once committed, changes survive crashes and power cuts.
Document stores (such as MongoDB) keep flexible JSON-like records.
Key-value stores (such as Redis) are very fast for caching and sessions.
Graph databases model networks such as social connections.
Column stores and data warehouses suit large analytical queries.

body.tip: Start with a well-designed relational database for most business systems; choose NoSQL for a specific need, not by fashion.

options: Links a row to a primary key in another table

options: A junction table such as enrolments
One table with a list of courses in a cell
